\paragraph{Depth-graduated data curation.}
Binary synthetic-data filters discard all machine-generated text indiscriminately, yet first-generation outputs may be benign or even beneficial for training \cite{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse}.
Our depth estimates offer a finer-grained alternative: predicted depth can serve as a continuous quality proxy for importance weighting in data curation pipelines such as DSIR \cite{dsir2023} and QuRating \cite{qurating2024}.
Rather than filtering at a binary threshold, a curation system could assign importance weights that decay with estimated depth \cite{sugiyama2007_importance_weighting}, retaining shallow-generation text while down-weighting deeply recursive samples.
We note this as a conceptual contribution---empirical validation of depth-weighted curation remains future work.

\paragraph{Feature evolution tracks tail erosion.}
Feature importance shifts with depth: \textsc{var\_surprisal} dominates at shallow recursions (d0 vs.\ d1), while \textsc{p90\_ppl} and kurtosis assume greater importance at deeper depths (d2+).
This progression---from second-order distributional changes to tail-shape collapse---aligns with the tail erosion theory of \citet{shumailov2024_nature} and the scaling-law analysis of \citet{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}.

\paragraph{Cross-strategy deployment requires strategy identification.}
The temperature-induced d1/d2 AUC inversion (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy})---as low as 0.13 for GPT-2~XL---means that deploying a depth estimator without knowing the target decoding strategy risks systematic prediction reversals.
Strategy-conditioned classifiers are a natural solution, though reliable strategy identification from text alone remains an open problem.

We introduced recursive generation depth estimation---the task of predicting how many model$\to$data$\to$model cycles a text passage has undergone---and demonstrated that lightweight statistical features suffice for reliable ordinal classification.
The Depth Degradation Atlas, spanning 3 model families $\times$ 3 decoding strategies $\times$ 4 depths, reveals a dual-layer signal structure: universal depth markers (90th-percentile perplexity and surprisal variance) that persist across all configurations, and strategy-dependent trajectories where temperature sampling accelerates convergence while top-$k$ attenuates the signal.
Our Effective Discriminable Depth metric ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$) quantifies the practical horizon of depth estimation.

In-distribution accuracy ranges from 70\% to 85\% across the atlas, with cross-model transfer at 66.4\% and cross-strategy transfer at 59.1\%.
The temperature-induced d1/d2 AUC inversion and the failure of end-to-end contrastive ordinal learning (DCOL; best 64.5\% vs.\ RF 78.2\%) highlight both the difficulty of the problem and the effectiveness of explicit statistical features.

Future work should address transfer to wild-data settings with mixed domains and instruction-tuned models, scaling beyond 1.5B parameters, strategy-conditioned classifiers that handle unknown decoding configurations, and empirical validation of depth-graduated data curation for training corpus quality management.
